Project OverviewThis project is my personal portfolio website. I built it so I could show my projects, resume, and a bit of my writing in one place.
I chose Hugo because it seemed like a good fit for a portfolio with a lot of content. It also made it easier to keep the structure clean and work in both English and Dutch without having to build everything twice.
I also learned Hugo by watching a few YouTube tutorials, which helped me get the basics faster and gave me a better idea of how to set up the site.
How I Built ItI started from a Hugo theme and then changed it step by step. The site is made up of content files, layout templates, CSS, and a bit of JavaScript.
The content is written in Markdown, so it stays easy to update. I also added bilingual content so visitors can switch between English and Dutch.
For the design, I used the Hugo Narrow theme as the base. After that, I adjusted the typography, spacing, navigation, and project cards so it felt more like my own portfolio.
Features Bilingual pages in English and Dutch Project, resume, and blog sections in one site Responsive layout for desktop and mobile Custom templates and styling on top of Hugo Fast static-site generation Easy content updates through Markdown Technologies UsedThe portfolio is built with Hugo, Markdown, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. I also used Git for version control and the Hugo theme structure as a starting point for the project.
Challenges and SolutionsOne challenge was keeping the site organized while supporting two languages. I solved that by separating the content into language-specific files and keeping the shared structure inside the templates.
Another challenge was making the portfolio feel less like a theme and more like my own site. I kept tweaking the layout and styling until it felt right.
Future Improvements Add more screenshots for each project Improve the visual storytelling on the home page Expand the project pages with more process details Keep refining the design as I add new work
summary: A portfolio website built with Hugo, custom layouts, and bilingual content.
title: My Portfolio with Hugo

On March 10, 2026, I took part in the Vibe Coding Hackathon, organized by Howest. It was a full day in which teams had to go from a vague idea to a working application. The fact that the event sold out immediately showed how much interest there was.
Unlike the previous Tech&Meet evenings, this was not a passive listening session, but a hands-on competition. The central concept was vibe coding: building software by guiding AI models such as Claude, GPT-4o, or Gemini through natural language instead of writing every line of code yourself. The event slogan summed it up well: you provide the vision, the AI does the heavy lifting.
The target audience was unusually broad: both IT students and business students were explicitly addressed. For IT students, the role shifts from bricklayer to architect: you focus on logic, security, and integrations. For business students, vibe coding opens a door that was often closed before: with tools like Lovable, you can build your own interfaces and flows without a technical background. That part was honestly one of the coolest ideas of the day, because you can go from idea to something real much faster.
Teams could choose from three tracks: a B2B automation solution (The Paperwork Killer), a local consumer app (The Hyper-Local Hero), or an interactive data dashboard (The Data Storyteller). The rule was clear: no PowerPoints, only a working demo by the end of the day. That pressure made it exciting and realistic.
What I learned goes beyond technical skills. Vibe coding forces you to think clearly about what you actually want to build: vague instructions produce vague results. It was an exercise in problem analysis, communication, and iterative thinking, all competencies that are sometimes underemphasized in education compared with pure coding knowledge.
At the same time, the rise of vibe coding also raises questions that the day itself did not fully answer: what about code quality, maintainability, and the security of AI-generated code? As an IT student, I think that critical layer is what separates us from someone who just works with prompts. It would be great if the program leaned into that more, for example by combining vibe coding with lessons on code review and technical debt.
Would I attend again? Absolutely. It was an energetic, inspiring day that broadened my view of software development. I would also strongly recommend it to fellow students, both from IT and business: that mix of profiles made the collaboration and conversations interesting and educational.

On November 18, 2025, I attended the .NET 10 Demystified session, hosted on the Howest campus in Bruges. It was a one-off two-hour evening session for developers and students who wanted to understand what the newest version of the .NET platform actually changes and what that means in practice.
The speaker was Kevin DeRudder, a familiar name in the Belgian .NET community. He is a full-stack web developer with a focus on ASP.NET and works as a trainer and coach. He is also one of the organizers behind Techorama, one of the largest developer conferences in Belgium and the Netherlands. He also speaks regularly at international conferences such as NDC. It quickly becomes clear that he not only has a lot of technical knowledge, but also knows how to explain it clearly.
The session focused on the most important new features in .NET 10: improvements in C#, updates to the runtime and libraries, tooling improvements, and better support for cloud-native applications. Kevin clearly wanted to separate the hype from the essentials, and he succeeded. The session was technical, but still easy to follow, even if you do not work with .NET every day.
What stayed with me most was the emphasis on practical applicability. Kevin illustrated each point with examples that fit realistic projects, such as enterprise applications, microservices, and AI integrations in .NET. That makes a real difference compared with a dry list of changelogs. You leave with insights you can use the next day.
The format of a short, focused evening session works well. Two hours is enough to explore a topic in depth without getting overwhelmed, and the location on the home campus lowers the barrier to attend. I would recommend this session to anyone who already works with .NET or plans to do so soon. I would definitely attend a future edition again myself.

Hack The Future is an annual hackathon organized by the Cronos Group, aimed at students in their final or penultimate year of an IT or creative program. The twelfth edition was centered around Aquatopia: a futuristic underwater world that ran as a common thread through all the challenges. I took part on day 1, the IT day, and worked with a fellow student on Flexso’s challenge: S.O.S. Abyss.
The scenario was set in the year 2550: an underwater base had been attacked, and we were the only survivors. The task was to restore the damaged systems, figure out what had gone wrong, and escape in time before the danger returned. Technically, the challenge used TypeScript, an MVC framework on the frontend, and Node.js as middleware. On paper it was a classic full-stack setup, but in practice it was mostly a race against the clock, with a storyline that made everything feel a bit more alive.
What stood out to me immediately was how thoughtfully the challenge was put together. Flexso is a Belgian company that works on SAP implementations and digital transformation, but for this hackathon they kept the stack approachable on purpose. I liked that: the day was about solving problems and working together, not about knowing some weird tool.
I already had experience with TypeScript and Node.js from my studies, but using that combination under time pressure in an unfamiliar codebase feels very different from a class project. You quickly notice how important it is to stay calm and actually talk to your teammate, instead of both of you sprinting in different directions. That was one of the biggest learning moments of the day for me.
The presence of coaches was a real plus. When we got stuck, we could simply ask them for help without it feeling like failure. On the contrary, there was clearly an atmosphere where asking questions was normal, and the organization actively encouraged that. That is a culture I would like to see in a work environment too.
As a whole, the event made a professional and well-organized impression. The atmosphere was energetic, and the location at Antwerp Zoo made it feel unique.
I would definitely do Hack The Future again, and I would also recommend it to fellow students. Not just for the technical challenge, but also for the networking and the realistic look into how IT companies think and work. For anyone who is hesitating: the barrier is lower than you might think, and you get a lot more out of it than you expect beforehand.

On November 5, 2025, I attended a Tech&Meet evening at Howest, organized by Cyber3Lab. The event lasted an hour and a half and focused entirely on Flutter, Google’s cross-platform framework. Just like the Hugging Face session a week earlier, it was part of the series of Tech&Meet evenings that Cyber3Lab regularly organizes for students and professionals. Flutter also has an active meetup community in Belgium.
The target audience was broad: developers, designers, and tech decision-makers who wanted to understand what “build once, deploy everywhere” means in practice. You could feel that in the atmosphere too: both students and professionals were present.
The speaker was Thijs Pirmez, an Android and iOS developer associated with Howest Cyber3Lab. Thijs has worked at Howest since May 2023, after an earlier career as a Project Engineer at BEP Europe NV. He is a self-taught developer who mainly focuses on Flutter for app development, but he also has experience with native Android development, front-end web, and AI research, especially object detection in mobile applications. The fact that he approached the topic from real project experience, rather than purely from theory, made his presentation credible and practical.
The event was clearly technical in nature. The session covered Flutter’s widget system, hot reload, integration with native code, and concrete app examples. Still, it remained accessible: even without prior knowledge of Flutter, you could follow the main ideas. I already had some basic knowledge of mobile development through my studies, but Flutter itself was mostly new to me. I found the idea of one codebase for iOS, Android, and web surprisingly powerful. Flutter makes it possible to use that single codebase directly across multiple platforms, which significantly reduces development time and maintenance.
What I learned most was how Flutter differs from native development, and why it can be a smart choice in many scenarios. The live demos helped make abstract concepts concrete. One small note: the session was compact, which meant that certain topics, such as Flutter’s weaknesses or more complex integrations, were covered a bit quickly. More depth on that critical side would have made the evening even more valuable.
Would I explore Flutter further? Definitely. It fits well with my interests in app development, and the low barrier to getting started makes it appealing to build projects with it myself. Would I attend the event again or recommend it? Absolutely, especially for anyone who wants to explore the mobile or cross-platform world. It is an approachable, high-quality way to connect with real-world practice and with people in the field.

On October 28, 2025, I attended a Tech&Meet evening at Howest, organized by Cyber3Lab. It was a two-hour session entirely dedicated to open-source AI and the Hugging Face ecosystem. This fits into the series of Tech&Meet evenings that Cyber3Lab regularly organizes for students and professionals.
The speaker was Niels Rogge, and his profile was genuinely impressive. He works as a machine learning engineer at ML6, a Belgian AI consultancy that implements generative AI solutions for large companies in the Benelux, Germany, and beyond. In addition, he works part-time at Hugging Face, where he is part of the open-source team. He has a special interest in NLP and contributes to open-source libraries such as the Hugging Face Transformers library, mainly working with deep learning models, PyTorch, and Google Colab. On X (Twitter), he now has more than 20,000 followers, which shows that he is a well-known voice in the international ML community. In short: someone with a lot of hands-on experience and a clear connection to the tools he spoke about.
The event was clearly technical in nature, but remained accessible to a broad audience: from beginners curious about AI to developers already working with machine learning. The focus on Hugging Face as a platform was a smart choice, because it is one of the most approachable entry points into open-source AI, with ready-to-use models, datasets, and tools.
What I learned included the difference between open-source and closed-source AI, and how organizations can use both. That nuance is often missing in education: we hear a lot about large commercial models like GPT, but the open-source alternatives and their practical applications get less attention. This event filled that gap in a meaningful way.
Would I attend this event again? Definitely. The combination of a strong speaker, relevant content, and the chance to network afterward makes it well worth it. I would also recommend it to fellow students, even to those without a technical background in AI: that broad accessibility is exactly what makes evenings like this valuable.
